boundary_evidence: Nasal intransitive versus stronger transitive formations recur independently in Tamil, Kannada, Telugu and the reconstruction.
input_support: Tamil aṭaŋku/aṭakku, Kannada aḍaŋgu/aḍaku and Telugu aḍãgu/aḍacu independently support the uncontracted low-vowel formative. K03 p.107 reconstructs these derivatives at Proto-South Dravidian level; PDr labels in CLDF are not precise historical levels.
direction_argument: The shared vowel-initial aṭ/aḍ order in SD I and aṛ- in Kurux–Malto, including the same stop/nasal formative contrasts, favors older *aṭ-aŋ- over an initial *ḍā- followed by multiple independent vowel insertions.
derivation: *aṭ-aŋ- > *aḍ-aŋ- > *ḍāŋ- > Telugu ḍā̃gu/dā̃gu; independently *aṭ-aŋkk- > *ḍāŋc- > ḍā̃cu/dā̃cu. Literal *ḍaaŋ- contraction and assimilation/stress-induced V1 loss are competing implementations; the Telugu nasal-loss and initial ḍ>d are subsequent developments.
exception_notes: Telugu retains aḍagu/aḍãgu “submit” and aḍacu “suppress” beside displaced “hide” forms: a real within-family semantic/formation split, not proof of a phonological exceptionless class. Kui also retains āṛpa/āṭpa. Kolami and Naikri are diagnosed as early Telugu loans by K03 p.107; aspiration in Naikri needs a recipient history. Tulu aḍeŋgɯ : ḍeŋgɯ/deŋguni is compatible with local aphaeresis, not independently the Telugu contraction. d80 shares compressed/piled semantics and homophonous Toda/Kannada evidence; sensitivity analysis should collapse d63+d80 without asserting that DEDR erred.
mechanism: Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

boundary_evidence: *-Vk expansion contrasts regionally with bare *aṭ-V; independent of metathesis outcome.
input_support: Tamil aṭi, Kannada aḍi and Telugu aḍugu support *aṭ- and different vowel/consonant formatives. K03-derived CLDF reconstructions explicitly leave V unspecified.
direction_argument: Initial vowel preceding the apical occurs in SD I and Gondi–Konda, supporting V–C order without using Telugu as the sole conservative witness.
derivation: *aṭ-Vk- > *aḍ-Vg- > Telugu aḍugu; Konda aḍgi shows medial-vowel loss without movement. Tamil/Kannada *aṭ-i gives aṭi/aḍi; they are not the identical -Vk derivative.
exception_notes: The independent suffix-vowel quality is not securely recovered: do not use Telugu u alone to prove a historical high-vowel class. Gadaba aḍugu is explicitly marked a Telugu loan. The Indo-Aryan heel forms attached to this family are contact comparisons, not votes for a Dravidian proto-vowel.
references: DEDR 72; K03 reconstruction records in Jambu
mechanism: Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

boundary_evidence: plausible formative boundary; not independently dated
input_support: Tamil aṭu/aṭi/aṭar and Kannada aḍi/aḍar establish short a and postvocalic retroflex; Telugu aḍucu and aḍupu retain that ordering. Kui ḍāmba and Kuvi ḍamb- support a labial nasal formative but do not independently establish Telugu *-aŋ-.
direction_argument: Independent SD I vowel-initial forms plus Parji/Gadaba aṭ(t)- support earlier V–ṭ; deriving them all by vowel insertion before Proto-*ḍa- is poorly motivated.
derivation: Possible *aṭ-aŋ- > *aḍ-aŋ- > *ḍāŋ- > ḍaŋgu > daŋgu, with shortening before NP; alternatively a consonantal formative produces short vowel directly. Transitive ḍancu/dancu and dampu have distinct extensions. Konda ḍaŋ-/ḍak-/ḍas- shows related displaced stems; exact shared suffixes require reconstruction.
exception_notes: Kui ā in ḍāmba supports investigating an early long vowel but is not an attested intermediate of Telugu ŋg. The Telugu non-displaced beat/fight forms must not be dropped. Tulu darpuni could reflect *aḍar- with aphaeresis, but the local vowel/stop history does not uniquely identify a literal swap. Kota ayṛ-/aṛc- is a distinct glide alternation.
references: K61 pp.53–54; PSS83 comparison of pound; DEDR 77
mechanism: Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

boundary_evidence: Derivative status of Telugu -ar- plausible from cross-language comparison; bare ability stems do not independently test the formative-conditioned rule.
input_support: Tamil aṭu, Malayalam aṭukka, Kannada aḍavu, Konda aṭ-, Pengo/Manda aḍ- support vowel-initial root. Telugu aḍaru has a different extension from the bare ability root.
direction_argument: Vowel-first root occurs in SD I, SD II and Malto, so the comparison supplies a broadly supported retained order.
derivation: *aṭ-V- > aḍ-/aṭ- in daughter languages; Telugu *aḍ-ar- > aḍaru. Kui/Kuvi āḍ- lengthens while retaining V–C; this is not metathesis.
exception_notes: A short-versus-long ability root alternation exists in Kuvi dialect/source records. Its quantity cannot be labeled concealed displacement because the apical remains postvocalic. Exact reconstruction of Telugu -ar- and whether it is productive morphology remain open.
mechanism: Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

boundary_evidence: The -ay- formation is supported by Tamil aṭai and Kannada aḍe; additional -ar/-Vk formations kept separate.
input_support: Tamil aṭai and Kannada aḍe support *aṭ-ay- independently; Tamil/Kannada aṭu/aḍar and aḍapu show distinct extensions. Long and short Telugu outcomes cannot all be assigned one suffix.
direction_argument: SD I aṭ/aḍ-initial bases and Malto aṭg- preserve V–apical ordering; Telugu ḍā- and Kui ṛā- are innovations under the cognacy hypothesis.
derivation: *aṭ-ay- > *aḍ-ay- > *ḍāy- > Telugu ḍāyu/dāyu; *aṭ-Vk- may yield *ḍak(k)- > ḍaggaṟa/daggaṟa, but the exact suffix and strengthening history are unresolved. Kui *aḍ-a-NC > ṛānja requires local ṭ/ṛ correspondence and is a separate derivation.
exception_notes: Telugu aḍaru “arise” retains order; a derived -k- nearness noun differs from the -ay- approach verb. Kuvi dagira/daggire/ḍagre resembles the Telugu extended nearness word and may be a loan; independently proving that donor history is necessary before counting an inherited Kuvi innovation. Kui retains aḍa/aṭpa beside ṛānja etc. No semantic label is used as an automatic phonological condition.
mechanism: Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

boundary_evidence: -uk(k) formation corroborated across Tamil/Malayalam/Telugu; root singleton is before the formative vowel.
input_support: Tamil aṭukku, Malayalam aṭukkuka, Telugu aḍuku independently support high u in a pile formation; Kannada aḍuku/aḍaku and Kodagu aḍak-/aḍaŋg- show vowel and transitivity variants.
direction_argument: All attested branches keep the root vowel before the apical. The medial cluster in Nilgiri forms is a syncope outcome, not initial apical movement.
derivation: *aṭ-ukk- > Tamil aṭukku; *aḍ-uk- > Telugu aḍuku; *aḍ-Vk- > Kota aṛk-/Toda oṛk-. No displacement is required for any reviewed reflex.
exception_notes: This is a retained high-formative counterpart to displaced high-formative cases elsewhere: vowel height alone does not decide application. The etymon overlaps d63 in Toda oṛk- “subdue, pile” and Kannada packing vocabulary. Report both strict DEDR counts and a conservative collapse with d63; do not count the same Toda token twice as independent root evidence.
mechanism: Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

boundary_evidence: plausible formative boundary; not independently dated
input_support: Telugu aḍugu and Parji aḍ-/aḍi support older vowel–apical order; Tamil aḷavu has a lateral and Tulu naṭṭu adds n and gemination. The precise PDr reconstruction is less secure than its starred CLDF display suggests.
direction_argument: Vowel-first Telugu and Parji agree, while Kui jāpa is analyzed in DEDR as an innovative reflex with a special ṭ : j correspondence. The disparate Tamil/Tulu roots prevent simply assuming all strings are regular descendants of one fully specified stem.
derivation: Telugu *aḍ-ug- > aḍugu retains order. Under DEDR cognacy, Kui *aṭ-a-p- > *ṭāp- > jāp- is a possible displacement derivation, requiring a low formative distinct from Telugu u and independent support for ṭ>j.
exception_notes: DEDR cites Burrow and Bhattacharya, IIJ 5:122 for ṭ : Kui j; that primary argument has not yet been obtained. The Kui history remains tentative, not a secure success in a quantitative sound-law test. Tamil lateral and Tulu n require either separate changes, morphological analysis, or revised cognacy.
references: DEDR 81, citing Burrow and Bhattacharya IIJ 5:122; Starostin via Merriam record 86
mechanism: Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

boundary_evidence: Support + stone composition independently visible in Tamil, Malayalam, Kannada and Telugu.
input_support: Tamil aṭai “support” and aṭai-kal “anvil”, Malayalam aṭa-kkallu and Kannada aḍe-gal/aḍa-gallu establish the support-stone compound independently of Telugu.
direction_argument: Vowel-first support nouns in three southern languages and Kota aṛ gal favor original *aṭay; Telugu initial ḍā is an innovation in the first compound member.
derivation: *aṭ-ay-kal > *aḍ-ay-kal > *ḍāy-kal > ḍā-kallu / ḍā-kali > dākali; dāyi can reflect the uncompounded first member. Intermediate y loss and changes of the stone component are separate from displacement.
exception_notes: This compound shows that a morphological boundary after the eligible first member need not block displacement. It does not license moving arbitrary consonants across a compound boundary. The detailed kali/gali/kallu variation needs suffix/compound history; it is not a free phonological substitution. No independent SCDr non-Telugu attestation is in this set.
mechanism: Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

boundary_evidence: plausible formative boundary; not independently dated
input_support: Tamil aracu/arai, Malayalam aracu/arayāl and Kannada arase/araḷi support initial ar-a- and several lexical extensions. K03 p.10 lists *ar-ac/-aḷ; those are not literal ancestors of Telugu rāvi.
direction_argument: Several SD I languages retain ar- and show internal suffix variation. The parsimonious directional comparison is ar-a- > rā-, but it does not independently reconstruct the final Telugu consonant.
derivation: *ar-a-... > *rā-... > rāvi/rāgi, with the -v/-g material unexplained by displacement itself. A specific *ar-avi or *ar-agi intermediate would be a fitted reconstruction and is not asserted.
exception_notes: Kannada rāvi is explicitly borrowed from Telugu. Kolami ra·vi and Konda rāyi maran could reflect contact with Telugu tree terminology; no independent chronology establishes separate innovations. Tamil arai already has a reduced extension, so later truncation is possible but does not explain all v/g/y correspondences.
mechanism: Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

boundary_evidence: Adjectival *-t- corroborated in Malayalam arutu and Telugu/Kannada arudu; not inferred from desired outcome.
input_support: Tamil aru/ariya, Malayalam arutu/ariya and Kannada arudu/aridu independently support a short ar- base with high-vowel extensions. Telugu arudu/aridi preserves both qualities.
direction_argument: All reviewed languages place a before r; there is no evidence for earlier initial r followed by inserted a.
derivation: *ar-u-tu > arudu in Telugu/Kannada, beside *ar-i- formations; Kota arg-/Toda arx- show ordinary loss of a medial high vowel. No displacement is required.
exception_notes: The bare root may be free, but the -t- nominal/adjectival formation is independently comparable and supplies a retained formative-bearing control. Tamil long āri etc. are root-quantity variants, not inferred metathesis stages. Kota “cry out in pain” appears as a separate lexicographic sense and is not used to reconstruct this family.
mechanism: Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

boundary_evidence: plausible formative boundary; not independently dated
input_support: Tamil arai, Malayalam arayuka and Kannada are/arayisu establish the ar-ay type independently. Telugu ṟ/r doublets need historical rhotic checking; their existence does not overturn the cross-language V–rhotic ordering.
direction_argument: The wide SD I ar- comparison and Gondi aṛs make vowel-first order preferable; Telugu rā- and several SCDr r-initial formations are innovative. The initial vowel cannot be restored merely from a hypothesized ban on initial r.
derivation: *ar-ay- > *rāy- > Telugu rāyu; strengthened/transitive derivatives give rācu/ṟācu and rāpu/ṟāpu. Different rē-/re- formations in Konda, Kui and Pengo require a vowel or suffix history beyond simple a+a contraction. Kui rāk-p- > rāpka illustrates separate stop metathesis after the initial displacement.
exception_notes: Telugu fragment nouns aravuḍu/aṟavaṟalu preserve order; ragulu/ravulu “kindle” have short a and semantic drift, so no unique long-to-short derivation is assumed. Kuvi mlekʰ'nai lacks a convincing segmental path from ar- and remains a questionable member. Gondi Koya rāy may be influenced by Telugu; Kolami rāk is a loan candidate. Malayalam rākuka beside irāvuka could arise by local aphaeresis plus v/k derivational variation. Neither southern nor central initial r automatically demonstrates shared inheritance.
references: DEDR 228; PSS83 pp.246–248 on independent southern aphaeresis
mechanism: Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

boundary_evidence: The historical separability of -ay is unproved; retain as a root-shape control instead of forcing the core classification.
input_support: Tamil arai, Kannada are, Telugu ara/aṟa and Naiki ar establish V–r ordering and the ay/a/e regional vowel correspondences.
direction_argument: The same ordering is widespread within SD I and retained in Telugu and Naiki. Nothing requires either a prior displacement or reinsertion.
derivation: *aray > Tamil arai, Kannada/Tulu are, Malayalam/Telugu ara; Kota/Toda/Naiki ar lose the final vowel. These changes do not relocate the rhotic.
exception_notes: This is a useful contrast to *ar-ay “grind”, but historical identity of the formative -ay is not proven: half may be a lexical free base, whereas grind enters verbal derivation. The distinction cannot be manufactured after noticing opposite outcomes. Telugu ṟ/r is recorded but its chronology remains unestablished.
mechanism: Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

boundary_evidence: -al in Telugu is recoverable conditionally from the older Tamil comparison, not independently from current DEDR descendants.
input_support: Gondi ar, Konda ar/arap and Pengo ar- support the vowel-first root. The -al required by Telugu rālu is not independently preserved in this current DEDR set; K61 p.56 compares Tamil aṟ-al, outside the present grouping.
direction_argument: Regional ar- stems independently favor earlier V–r order. Telugu rāl- has an added lateral formation; the Koya rāl loan cannot be counted as independent support for its antiquity.
derivation: If the older -al comparison is accepted, *ar-al- > *rāl- > Telugu rālu, with causative rāl-p-/rāl-c-. Pengo ar- : rat- suggests displacement in a derived causative. Kuvi rī- and Manda re- cannot be predicted from *ar-al; their formations and vowel histories remain separate.
exception_notes: Gondi rāl is explicitly labeled from Telugu. Kolami/Naikri rāl- forms are probable contact comparanda but have not been independently dated. K61 source comparison must be checked before *ar-al is treated as a secure low-vowel input. A shared abstract “fall” meaning does not make every derivative identical.
mechanism: Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

boundary_evidence: -ay and nasal extensions are independently attested; lampaṭa segmentation remains unresolved.
input_support: Tamil alai/alaŋku, Malayalam alayuka/alaŋŋuka, Telugu alayu/alãgu independently supply short al-a- and extended stems. The CLDF negative *al “be not” is not evidence for this lexical family.
direction_argument: SD I, Telugu, Kolami and Parji agree on initial al-; r/l-initial variants need their own histories rather than a uniform reconstructed initial liquid.
derivation: Retained *al-a-y > Telugu alayu and *al-aŋ- > alãgu. Telugu lampaṭa and Kannada lampaṭe admit initial-vowel loss or contact-related restructuring; their exact earlier compound is unknown. Kui laha may reflect loss/reordering from al-a-, but short a and h are not fully explained.
exception_notes: DEDR explicitly separates Sanskrit-derived Telugu lampaṭũḍu from the trouble noun and tentatively proposes Dravidian > Sanskrit borrowing for lampaṭa. This can involve export and reborrowing, not a simple one-way loan label. Kurux layā- vs algā requires separate suffix and vowel analysis. A bogus Malto alaŋku row is actually the opening of DEDR editorial prose about Tamil; only Malto alesi is lexical evidence. DEDR warns that d236 “suffer” and d240 “move” have converged semantically; separate roots remain the primary partition, with a collapsed sensitivity analysis.
references: DEDR 236 and preserved editorial comparison; PSS83 pp.246–248
mechanism: Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

boundary_evidence: plausible formative boundary; not independently dated
input_support: Tamil/Malayalam alaku and Kannada alagu/alugu establish vowel-first lateral and an extended stem; Telugu alũgu has nasalization and high medial u.
direction_argument: All witnesses retain a before l. Vowel change and nasalization in Telugu are not evidence that earlier metathesis has occurred.
derivation: *al-ak- > alaku/alagu, beside *al-uk- > alugu and Telugu alũgu; no apical relocation. The origin of nasalization needs source or derivative evidence.
exception_notes: Root/formative segmentation is plausible but not established by a corresponding bare *al “blade”. Keep exact V2 classification variable, not a chosen vowel tailored to expected length. The root is phonologically eligible if that segmentation is accepted; retention itself does not establish non-eligibility.
mechanism: Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

boundary_evidence: -ay and -aŋ/-uk formations independently visible in SD I; exact Pengo/Irula formations unknown.
input_support: Tamil alai/alaŋku, Malayalam alayuka/alaŋŋuka and Kannada ale/alagu supply medial l and low formative independently; Telugu ala and allāḍu preserve the order.
direction_argument: The shared vowel-first SD I/Telugu base plus Kurux alr- favors original al-. Kui lāng- is a derived innovative outcome, not a reason to reverse the reconstructed comparison.
derivation: *al-aŋ- > *lāŋ- > Kui lānga; its causative lāk-p- > lāpka requires separate stop-cluster metathesis. Telugu allāḍu can be analyzed as a reinforced/reduplicated formation associated with “move” and must not be reduced to an imaginary initial *lā-. Pengo lem- and Irula le·- require a separate vowel and derivative history.
exception_notes: Tulu landuni/landele may show independent aphaeresis in a wanderer derivative; no shared SCDr event follows. Pengo e and Irula e· cannot be generated by simple a+a contraction without another change. Malayalam alaŋŋ-/anaŋŋ- is l/n assimilation/variation, not vowel–liquid displacement. DEDR treats this root as originally distinct from d236 but acknowledges semantic convergence.
mechanism: Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

boundary_evidence: Different final extensions support segmentation only provisionally.
input_support: Tulu aḍakuni and Telugu aḍarucu/aḍarincu agree in aḍa-, with different final extensions. The database PSTDr reconstruction rests on only this two-language comparison.
direction_argument: Both comparative members are vowel-initial; no independent displaced member motivates an earlier alternative order.
derivation: *aṭ-a-r- > aḍarucu in Telugu; *aṭ-a-k- > aḍakuni in Tulu, conditionally on cognacy. No vowel/apical exchange is necessary.
exception_notes: A low second vowel is directly shared, but the narrow distribution and final r:k mismatch limit the reconstruction level. The contrast is retained as a narrow comparison, not elevated to secure PDr evidence.
mechanism: Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

boundary_evidence: Areca + bag comparison is explicit in DEDR 88; probable cultural diffusion is not independently dated.
input_support: Tamil aṭappam/aṭaippam, Malayalam aṭappam and Kannada aḍapa support aṭ-a-pp-. DEDR 88 supplies Tamil aṭaippai and explicitly cross-refers to this pouch family.
direction_argument: All daughter forms retain the vowel before ṭ/ḍ. Optional h in Kannada, Tulu and Telugu does not reverse the vowel/apical sequence.
derivation: *aṭay-ppay (areca + bag) > aṭappam/aṭaippam and aḍapa-mu, with compounding and nominal-final alternation. The exact relation of pp-ay to -ppam needs separate morphology; no metathesis is needed.
exception_notes: Count together with d88, since the pouch is an areca compound and d88 actually repeats its Tamil form and Telugu derivatives. h-prothesis may mark regional transmission, but is not alone proof of a particular loan direction. This cultural vocabulary supplies an attested retention comparison with uncertain inheritance chronology.
mechanism: Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

boundary_evidence: plausible formative boundary; not independently dated
input_support: Kannada aḍigera, Telugu aṭika and Gondi aṛka/aṭkā suggest *aṭ-Vk-. Tulu aḍḍyara and Kurux aṛī have different extensions; reconstruction of one fully specified word is unwarranted.
direction_argument: SD I, Telugu, Gondi and Kurux agree on V–apical ordering, independently supporting a vowel-initial base.
derivation: *aṭ-ik- > aṭika is compatible with Telugu, but i is not securely common to all extensions; *aṭ-Vk- > Gondi aṛka/aṭkā illustrates medial syncope. No initial displacement.
exception_notes: Tulu gemination and the final r/k correspondence require formation-level history. Gondi Chanda adka and aṛka include broken editorial gloss fragments; use the securely glossed dialect rows for semantics. Pot terminology could diffuse, so inheritance at PDr level remains provisional.
mechanism: Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

boundary_evidence: Root singleton versus tense/noun gemination is independently supported by Tamil and Kannada paradigms; compounds not treated as independent roots.
input_support: Tamil aṭu (aṭuv-, aṭṭ-), Malayalam aṭuka and Kannada aḍu (aṭṭ-) support singleton *aṭ- and high-vowel verb formations independently of the geminate food noun *aṭṭu displayed at the DEDR head.
direction_argument: Both southern and south-central languages have vowel-initial roots, including Kui aṭa and Kuvi aṭ. An initial ṭ reconstruction would require unmotivated widespread prothesis.
derivation: *aṭ-u- > retained cooking verbs; tense/noun strengthening yields aṭṭ- and Telugu aṭṭu. Telugu aḍugaṇṭu retains the singleton in a compound. Kui aṭa and Konda aṭk- retain order in heat/burn formations.
exception_notes: The pancake head is not the only reconstructed input of this etymon. Counting all members as geminate-root exclusions would discard eligible singleton derivatives. Conversely the geminate pancake alone does not test movement of a singleton. Telugu aḍasāla contains a separate kitchen component and may be regionally transmitted. Badaga aṭra/attara hot variants require local cluster/epenthesis history, not the initial metathesis examined here; nāgaṭṭte plant name has uncertain linkage.
references: DEDR 76; K03 pancake reconstruction in CLDF
mechanism: Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

boundary_evidence: Singleton -ay verbal root and strengthened crosswise noun supported across SD I; root-family relation plausible but not a license to erase stem distinctions.
input_support: Tamil aṭai and Malayalam aṭayuka support singleton *aṭ-ay, while Tamil aṭṭam, Kannada aḍḍa and Telugu aḍḍamu independently support a strengthened transverse/obstruction formation. Both must be represented.
direction_argument: Numerous SD I and SD II forms retain initial a. Initial ḍ in Kui ḍākoli could be displaced, but the word is not segmentally identical to the native simple closing stems and needs independent history.
derivation: Retained *aṭay > Tamil aṭai / Tulu aḍe-vuni; strengthened *aṭṭa > Telugu aḍḍa(mu). Telugu aḍucu-konu retains the singleton in a derived construction. Hypothetical *aṭ-a-k... > *ḍāk... for Kui shield remains unverified.
exception_notes: Do not classify the entire etymon as a geminate blocker from Telugu aḍḍa alone. Kui aḍa is explicitly said to be from Oriya; ḍākoli shield could be inherited, compounded or borrowed, with no independently recovered complete input. Brahui āṛ and Malto aṛatre have explicit IA doubts. The broad IA obstruction series is contact evidence, not extra independent Dravidian controls. Kuvi kīnai is an extracted light verb, not a standalone cognate of aṭ-.
mechanism: Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

boundary_evidence: plausible formative boundary; not independently dated
input_support: Tamil aṭai/aṭar, Kannada aḍe/aḍar and Telugu aḍaru establish short a, singleton apical and low vowel extensions. These are independent of the strengthened pile nouns.
direction_argument: SD I, Telugu, Konda aḍar and Pengo aḍer all put a before the apical; no reversal is required.
derivation: *aṭ-ar- > aḍaru in Telugu and aḍar in Kannada/Konda. *aṭ-ay- > aṭai/aḍe; strengthened *aṭṭ- appears in pile nouns. Pengo e after the apical is a local vowel development without displacement.
exception_notes: Telugu eṭṭam differs in V1, and aṭṭaḍi/aṭṭava have strengthened compound-like shapes: these are not examples of initial displacement. The root is semantically close to pile d80 and approach d79; audit an alternative broad family collapse rather than treating semantic similarity as proof of one root.
mechanism: Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

boundary_evidence: Fruit, bag and tool components compared independently; root is shared with d64.
input_support: Tamil aṭaikkāy, Malayalam aṭakka/aṭekka and Kannada aḍake support the areca + fruit compound; Kannada aḍa and tool compounds support a reduced first member independently.
direction_argument: Vowel-first ordering is supported by several SD I languages. Koraga initial ḍ can arise by loss of initial a in a locally contracted areca word, without importing a Telugu history.
derivation: *aṭay-kkāy > aṭaikkāy / aḍake, then in Tappu Koraga *aḍakke > ḍakke by aphaeresis and local compound reduction. Telugu aḍa-katti etc. retain the first member; aḍḍa-kattera has additional strengthening.

Telugu has tools/bag attendants, not the identical inherited fruit noun; contact among areca-using communities remains plausible. Kannada Areca catecʰu is a botanical Latin fragment misparsed as a Kannada form and is excluded. Count d64+d88 once as the areca/bag family.
references: DEDR 88,64; K03 SD I areca reconstruction
mechanism: Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

boundary_evidence: Opaque internal segmentation; no outcome-based boundary is invented.
input_support: Tamil aṭaiyāḷam, Malayalam aṭayāḷam and Kannada aḍayāḷa agree in a long word; Telugu has aḍiyālamu. The inherited morpheme structure is not independently established.
direction_argument: All comparison languages have a before the apical. The Toda source explicitly compares Tamil, so Toda is not an independent proto-stage witness.
derivation: Regional aṭayāḷam > aḍayāḷa / aḍiyālamu is a plausible transmission/adaptation series; exact vowel, lateral and direction of loans need separate evidence. No displacement is required.
exception_notes: Do not use the starred database PSTDr string as proof of ancient inheritance. This word may have spread after the sound change or contain an ineligible boundary. Neither explanation is established by its retained outcome, so it remains outside the decisive inherited denominator.
references: DEDR 89; Emeneau 1984 p.10 via Toda record
mechanism: Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

boundary_evidence: Telugu -pp- is a possible formative, not independently recovered from the compared stems.
input_support: Kannada nīr-aṛ̆ke/nīr-aḍike, Kolami aḍḍ-, Naikri aḍ and Parji/Gadaba anḍ suggest a vowel-initial apical base, but disagree on apical identity and pre-apical nasal/gemination. Starostin marks the reconstruction questionable.
direction_argument: All non-Telugu comparanda favor a before an apical; Telugu ḍappi could be displaced if the comparison is correct. Their divergent consonants prevent a unique detailed proto-form.
derivation: Conditional *aḍ-p- > *ḍa-pp- > ḍappi > dappi, with formative strengthening, is compatible with the short vowel. An older nasal or *ẓ requires different consonant developments. No *aḍa- input is inserted just to predict ā and then explain it away.
exception_notes: This is evidence for investigating displacement, but not a secure geminate exception or proof of a low-vowel shortening rule. Kannada aṛ̆ is a distinct historical apical, while Parji/Gadaba have a nasal. Etymon d277 also contains ḍappi in the sense distress/perishing: evaluate lexical conflation and possible semantic overlap. A primary source paradigm for thirst dayyu and an early dated ḍappi would help separate analyses.
mechanism: Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

boundary_evidence: Sanskrit nominal stem and recipient nominal/compound morphology.
input_support: DEDR explicitly derives the family from Sanskrit rājan-. K03 pp.476–477 independently identifies Tamil aracan and Kannada arasu as early adapted loans with prothetic a. Toda source explicitly says Kannada/Sanskrit borrowing.
direction_argument: Comparative direction is donor r-initial > recipient ar-initial, not Proto-Dravidian ar- > r-. Modern initial a in several Dravidian languages therefore does not establish inherited a-r ordering.
derivation: Sanskrit rājan- > regional *arāca- > araca(n)/arasu/arusu, with prothesis, quantity adaptation, intervocalic consonant adaptation and recipient endings. Intermediate recipient steps are schematic; a single shared borrowing episode is not established.
exception_notes: The PSTDr starred database head is a regional comparison, not evidence that this is inherited PDr. Telugu rāju elsewhere is not automatically a metathesized doublet of arusu: separate Sanskrit loan strata must be tested. DEDR cites a 2nd-century Śātavāhana coin form arahaṇasha, but identifies its language as unknown and only presumably South Dravidian; it cannot securely date specifically Telugu metathesis.
references: DEDR 201 editorial note; K03 pp.476–478; Sircar 1961 EI 35:247–252 cited by DEDR (not independently checked)
mechanism: Prothesis and loan adaptation, not inherited apical displacement

boundary_evidence: Botanical stem segmentation opaque.
input_support: Telugu araṭi/araṇṭi/arãṭi and anaṇṭi/anãṭi/aṇṭi provide internal variation. The only non-Telugu evidence, Gondi arṭi, is explicitly marked borrowed from Telugu; K03 labels the reconstruction SD II, but the current set does not independently justify a shared proto-stage.
direction_argument: Telugu variants favor an older r-containing local stem, but no independent inherited cognate establishes exact early segment order or V2. The Gondi loan reproduces recipient syncope after borrowing.
derivation: Within the local family araṇṭi > arãṭi/araṭi is compatible with nasal weakening/loss; araṇṭi > anaṇṭi suggests regressive nasal assimilation; reduction gives aṇṭi. Relative order of these reductions is not uniquely recoverable.
exception_notes: No initial *rā- reflex occurs, and the loss of r in aṇṭi does not require concealed metathesis. Treat as a single-language reconstruction problem, not an independently reconstructed unchanged success. The Kittel-only variants may preserve valuable dialect history; independent historical spellings could decide the r/n chronology.
references: DEDR 205; K03 SD II reconstruction in CLDF
mechanism: Nasal assimilation, nasal loss and stem reduction; no displacement demonstrated

boundary_evidence: Final lateral may be a formative, but independent morphological status is unknown.
input_support: Tamil aril and Telugu aralu independently provide initial ar- plus a later lateral. Telugu allu and Salur Gadaba all lack the rhotic. Tamil i versus Telugu a prevents recovering one exact medial vowel.
direction_argument: The rhotic-bearing Tamil and Telugu forms favor an earlier ar-V-l sequence; rhotic assimilation after medial syncope produces ll more economically than a vowel–rhotic swap followed by reinsertion of initial a.
derivation: *ar-V-l- > *ar-l- > *al-l- > Telugu allu, Gadaba all, conditional on cognacy. Telugu aralu retains the longer formation. This orders vowel loss before rl assimilation, but does not independently date either.
exception_notes: The lexeme may be related to weaving d260; evaluate a merged family sensitivity because allu occurs in both with closely related senses. The r-bearing witnesses prevent automatically treating every all- as original geminate l. Whether Gadaba borrowed Telugu allu rather than inherited the assimilation remains open.
mechanism: Medial syncope and rhotic–lateral assimilation; not initial displacement

boundary_evidence: plausible formative boundary; not independently dated
input_support: Tamil ari and Telugu ari agree in the tax noun; Telugu aruvu supplies another rhotic formation. The relationship of Kannada/Telugu accu and Telugu appu to these nouns is not a regular consequence of metathesis.
direction_argument: Vowel-first ari is independently supported, but it does not alone reconstruct the entire debt series. A hypothetical *ar-pp > appu requires assimilation and a separately motivated formative, not initial-r movement.
derivation: *ari > retained tax noun. Conditional *ar-pp- > *app- > appu and *ar-cc- > *acc- > accu invoke regressive assimilation or loss of the rhotic after suffix combination. Their exact formative origins are unresolved. No initial *rV- stage is necessary.
exception_notes: DEDR cross-refers to d223 arukku take, snatch, demand; that may explain the payment verb semantically, but must be reviewed before a single derivation is accepted. Tamil appu and Kuvi aruvu/aṛvū are explicit Telugu loans. They do not independently corroborate a common *ar-pp stage.
mechanism: Possible suffix-triggered cluster assimilation, not evidence for apical displacement

boundary_evidence: Bare aru and parallel -k/-v extensions support root/formative distinction without recourse to outcomes.
input_support: Tamil aruku/aruvu, Malayalam ariku/aruvu and Kannada arugu/arigu independently show short ar- and high-vowel extensions; Telugu arugu and aṟu/aṟuta have rhotic spelling variation.
direction_argument: Multiple southern languages place the root vowel before r. Telugu agrees; no displacement or restoration of an earlier displaced form is demanded.
derivation: *ar-uk- > aruku/arugu; *ar-uv- > aruvu; short base *ar-u > aṟu and related locative/adverbial extensions. Telugu arudencu contains additional come/go morphology rather than a reversed root.
exception_notes: Kannada aragu has a low-vowel variant, and Gondi araluk is a more extended close/follow expression; neither can be used to assign the same historical V2 to all forms. Kurux arbar-parbar is a paired/echo expression with uncertain exact cognacy. Telugu ṟ/r history needs early spellings, but both preserve vowel-first order.
mechanism: Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

boundary_evidence: Historical separability of -uḷ is unproved.
input_support: Tamil aruḷ, Malayalam aruḷ and Telugu arulu independently support the two-liquid stem, with Telugu merger of retroflex lateral. Kota arḷ has medial vowel loss.
direction_argument: The ordering ar-u-ḷ is common to the southern and Telugu evidence; Kota syncope supports loss of the medial vowel rather than a shift of the rhotic to the start.
derivation: *aruḷ > Telugu arulu, with ḷ>l; *aruḷ > Kota arḷ by syncope. Neither change requires metathesis. Date and direction of possible religious vocabulary transmission are unknown.
exception_notes: The source compares d381 ārvam and tentatively d203 araṇa; neither proves a productive -uḷ formative. Treat this as an eligible root-shape comparison with uncertain morphological status, not an invented free-root exception. Affection and divine utterance differ semantically but have ordinary potential links through favor/command.
mechanism: Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

boundary_evidence: plausible formative boundary; not independently dated
input_support: Kota and Toda arb have r before b; Telugu abbu and Kuvi abbinai have a geminate b and compatible enjoyment/prosperity semantics. The shared Nilgiri form is not independent evidence for a particular lost vowel.
direction_argument: If cognate, arb > abb by assimilation is preferable to reconstructing initial r and then losing it while restoring a. The current evidence does not determine whether rb was original or produced by syncope.
derivation: *ar(V)b- > *arb- > abb- > Telugu abbu, conditionally on cognacy. Kuvi abb- may share assimilation or be influenced by Telugu. No initial apical displacement is needed.
exception_notes: The reconstructed boundary and vowels are unknown; label this a probable competing mechanism, not a regular retained liquid outcome. Nilgiri extreme happiness versus Telugu acquire/Kuvi prosper is semantically plausible but not proof. An uncontracted matching derivative outside Nilgiri or early Kuvi evidence would strengthen the comparison.
mechanism: Probable rb assimilation, with syncope optional and cognacy provisional

boundary_evidence: No secure independent formative boundary; reconstructed nasal cluster is only a hypothesis.
input_support: Kannada alabu/alubu and Telugu alamu agree on vowel-first al-, but b:m and a:u variation do not uniquely support the full starred *alamb- supplied in CLDF. Gondi allam is explicitly a Telugu loan.
direction_argument: The two non-identical comparison stems both preserve a before l. There is no displaced form from which an earlier reversed order can be independently inferred.
derivation: A regional *al-Vmb- could yield Kannada alabu and Telugu alamu by different cluster reductions, but neither the nasal cluster nor a common V2 is securely attested. No metathesis is required.
exception_notes: Botanical identifications and semantic breadth need primary lexicographic checking. The Kannada Latin genus record Alysicarpus is a parsing artifact. This narrow comparison is useful for recording uncertainty, not for proving a PDr unchanged control.
mechanism: Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

boundary_evidence: Distinct -pp/-mp/-ṟ verbal extensions independently compared; Telugu suffixes are not forced into the same shape.
input_support: Tamil alappu/alampu/alaṟu, Malayalam alappu/alaṟuka and Old Kannada alaṟu support a low-vowel initial al-a- base independently. Telugu has different alikiḍi/alabalamu formations.
direction_argument: Independent southern arousal/noise stems support a before l; Irula lā·ru is plausibly an innovative initial-loss/contraction outcome of the roaring derivative.
derivation: *al-aṟ- > alaṟu in Tamil/Old Kannada; possible *alaṟ- > *lāṟ- > Irula lā·ru. This could involve vowel coalescence with apical displacement or aphaeresis and compensatory lengthening. Telugu alikiḍi has a high-vowel extension not identical to the roaring stem.
exception_notes: Do not group by expressive meaning to exempt words from sound change: the morphological and segmental inputs still need reconstruction. Malayalam aḷavan boaster is explicitly an alternative comparison with measure d296, so retroflex ḷ is not silently regularized to l. Irula length and donor/native status require a local source history before counting a shared SCDr innovation.
mechanism: Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

boundary_evidence: -ay, -mp, -kk and -k extensions have independent southern evidence; no single suffix is assigned to all.
input_support: Tamil alaicu/alampu, Malayalam alakkuka/alampuka and Kannada ale/alambu independently support vowel-first al- and low-vowel formations. Kannada alumbu and Telugu aluku supply high-vowel variants.
direction_argument: Southern cognates favor earlier initial al-. Tulu lumbuni can be derived directly from the attested alumbuni by aphaeresis; Kui akali requires a different account of k and l positions.
derivation: *al-amp- > retained alamp-/alamb-; *al-ump- > Tulu alumbuni > lumbuni by initial a loss. Telugu alãdu and aluku have separate consonantal extensions. Conditional *al-akk- > *ak-al- > Kui akali would be nonadjacent consonant transposition, but the exact input/formation is not independently established.
exception_notes: Tulu retains u after l and a nasal cluster, so an initial vowel/stop exchange is unnecessary. Kui akali is genuinely printed in a Kui vocabulary, with akali-pakali and light-verb constructions; it is not merely a Jambu typo. The existence of that noun does not prove its DEDR etymology. Toda as̱p- lacks l and may involve a local lateral-plus-stop development; its exact history must be checked separately.
references: DEDR 246; Winfield 1929, A Vocabulary of the Kui Language, p.3; NBU handle 123456789/1942 (title and entry visually checked)
mechanism: Retentions plus independent aphaeresis; possible other consonant metathesis in Kui

boundary_evidence: Whether -ar is a separable formative is unresolved; the consonant order is directly comparable.
input_support: Tamil alar, Malayalam alar and Telugu alaru support older l...r order, independently of Kannada/Tulu variants. Kannada retains alar beside aral/araḷ, so both orders occur within one language.
direction_argument: Concordant l...r in Tamil, Malayalam and Telugu plus retained Kannada alar favors *alar > aral, not *aral as the uniform family input. There is no evidence that the initial vowel has moved.
derivation: *alar > Kannada/Tulu aral by nonadjacent consonant metathesis; *aral > araḷ by a separate lateral change. Kannada alal may instead reflect r-to-l assimilation. Kannada arlu involves medial syncope, plausibly after the r...l ordering had developed.
exception_notes: This is a real comparative metathesis candidate outside Telugu, but a different process from initial apical promotion. R in the main outcome matrix means the target initial V–apical order remains; an orthogonal process annotation records the l/r exchange. DEDR tentatively relates beauty d248, which must be collapsed in a conservative family sensitivity. Marathi araḷ/arala is a contact comparison, not an independent Dravidian language vote.
references: DEDR 247 and editorial cross-references to DEDR 248 and Marathi
mechanism: Nonadjacent l...r > r...l metathesis in Kannada/Tulu; no initial-vowel displacement

boundary_evidence: plausible formative boundary; not independently dated
input_support: Tamil alari and Telugu alarincu/alarāru support al-ar; Kannada alampu has a different labial/nasal extension and lampu lacks initial a.
direction_argument: Vowel-first ordering is supported by the Tamil/Telugu comparison and by Kannada alampu itself. The lampu variant is therefore an innovation, without requiring a displaced shared proto-root.
derivation: Kannada alampu > lampu by aphaeresis gives the attested short a directly. Telugu alarāru is an extended shine/suit verb retaining initial al-; its internal long vowel is not evidence of initial metathesis.
exception_notes: DEDR tentatively cross-refers to blossom d247; the overlapping shine/rejoice semantics suggest a derivative relationship, but do not prove it. Treat root-family merging as a sensitivity test. Kannada -mp versus -r needs a derivative or cognacy account independent of aphaeresis.
mechanism: Local Kannada aphaeresis, not proof of SCDr vowel–apical metathesis

reconstruction: Telugu ala-vaḍ-/ala-vaṟ-; earlier independent base unknown
boundary_evidence: Local compound/derivative segmentation plausible, proto-stage not independently recovered.
input_support: Telugu ala-vaḍu, ala-vaṟucu and ala-vāṭu show local derivative alternation. The Tamil alavāṭṭu is explicitly borrowed from Telugu, so it supplies no independent earlier input.
direction_argument: The current evidence gives only a local vowel-first stem, not a comparative proof of a Proto-South-Central *ala-. The database starred PSD2 root overstates what this isolated group can establish.
derivation: Telugu ala-vaḍu : ala-vaṟucu : ala-vāṭu exhibits verb/causative/nominal morphology. No initial consonant movement is observed; chronology and origin of the first component are unknown.
exception_notes: This cannot become a secure retained sound-law counterexample merely because it looks like ala-. Conversely, absence of independent cognates does not prove it entered Telugu too late for the sound change. A dated early compound and independently cognate first member would resolve eligibility.
mechanism: Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

boundary_evidence: Consonantal -k may be an instrument/product formative; relationship to weaving supported by semantics and source cross-reference.
input_support: Parji alka and Telugu alle/alliya support al- plus a possible consonantal extension; DEDR explicitly cross-refers to weave d260.
direction_argument: Both languages keep the initial vowel. If the forms are cognate, lk > ll accounts for Telugu without moving l across the vowel.
derivation: *al-k- > alka in Parji; *alk- > *all- > alle/alliya in Telugu with progressive cluster assimilation and nominal-final development. A stem without *k plus distinct formations is also possible.
exception_notes: Count together with weave d260 in the conservative main family partition; the bowstring is a plausible woven-product noun, not automatically a separate root. The absence of an attested Telugu k-bearing precursor keeps the assimilation route conditional.
mechanism: Possible progressive cluster assimilation; no initial apical displacement

boundary_evidence: Consonantal p/t and tense allomorphs independently documented in Konda, Kui and Kolami; geminate southern stems are kept distinct.
input_support: Kolami al-, Konda al-/aṛ-, Kui alpa and Kuvi al- support a singleton lateral root and consonantal extensions. Tamil/Kannada/Telugu allu is a strengthened formation, not proof that the entire proto-root was geminate.
direction_argument: SD I, SD II and Central Dravidian agree on an initial vowel before the lateral. There is no evidence that the root began l- and acquired a independently in every branch.
derivation: *al-p- > Konda/ Kui alpa; *al-t- gives relevant tense/extended clusters; strengthened *all- > Telugu/Tamil/Kannada allu. Konda al- : aṭ-/aṇ- reflects separately conditioned tense allomorphy. None requires initial movement.
exception_notes: Five forms assigned Gondi in the corpus are actually under the Konda heading in DEDR p.25; research corrections are ID-specific and preserve original labels. The only genuine Gondi form is Koya all-. Brahui allī has an explicit source question mark and cannot prove inherited North Dravidian cognacy. Bowstring d259 is conservatively one root family; creeper d207 is a further uncertain relationship, with r-bearing evidence that could indicate a different earlier root.
references: DEDR 260 p.25 and 259; original DSAL p.25 directly inspected
mechanism: Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

boundary_evidence: Low -al and high -uŋk independently distinguished; Konda/Kuvi extensions are not assigned an invented vowel to fit their outputs.
input_support: Tamil aṛ̆al and Malayalam aṛ̆aluka support *aẓ-al independently; Tamil aṛ̆uŋku supports a different high-vowel nasal extension. Old Kannada aṛ̆v and Tulu arluni corroborate the vowel-first root. The database head **aẓVnkV is not the sole reconstructed formation.
direction_argument: The southern comparison favors V–ẓ order for the regional input. DEDR tentatively connects initial t-bearing fire vocabulary d3115: that would place earlier initial-consonant loss before the regional vowel-initial stage, but is not established by this set alone.
derivation: *aẓ-al > Telugu aḍalu/aḍaru with ẓ>ḍ and final-liquid variation, without initial displacement. Kannada aẓ-kaj > akkaja illustrates cluster assimilation. Conditional *aẓ-V-mp > *ẓV̄mp > Konda ṛīmbu would require an independently justified high-vowel history; the modern ī is not sufficient to reconstruct that history.
exception_notes: Konda ember and Kuvi blaze/light forms begin ṛī-, compatible with displacement but with unexplained vowel quality and different extensions. Gondi eṛki/eṛk explicitly carries DEDR’s warning that its vowel is difficult. Kota arl fever has an alternative d214 comparison. Tamil aṭalai and Kannada aḍalu/aṛ̆al are source-marked Telugu loans. Kurux aŋgnā may lose ẓ in a medial cluster; it is not evidence of initial relocation.
references: DEDR 276 and its comments on d214,281,3115
mechanism: Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

boundary_evidence: Tamil tense and transitivity morphology independently supports i plus labial versus dental strong extensions; K03 reconstructs nasal precursors.
input_support: Tamil aṛ̆i with transitive -pp-/-tt-, Malayalam aṛ̆iyuka/aṛ̆ikka and Kannada aṛ̆i/aṛ̆ipu independently support high i and vowel-first ẓ. K03 p.195 explicitly derives Telugu destruction forms from non-past *aẓ-i-mpp and past *aẓ-i-ntt.
direction_argument: SD I and Gondi vowel-first stems, together with retained Telugu aṛ̆isina/aṛ̆ipuṭa, favor earlier aẓi-. Inscriptional Telugu ṛ̆accu has initial ẓ while still preserving its identity: displacement need not wait until ẓ has become ḍ.
derivation: K03: *aẓ-i-ntt > *aẓ-i-cc > inscriptional ẓaccu; *aẓ-i-mpp > *ẓapp- > Telugu ḍappi. Palatalization after i must precede deletion of its conditioning vowel under this account. Initial ẓ>ḍ follows displacement in the labial formation; the inscriptional palatal formation directly attests the otherwise hidden initial-ẓ stage. These are related tense/voice formations, not two independent sound-change events.
exception_notes: Sastri 1969 pp.310–311, inscription38 (dated there 890 CE), has displaced ḻassi line14 and retained aḻisina lines20–21, aḻiputa line35 in one text, but different grammatical formations: coexistence is not identical-context free variation. Earlier inscription16 (pp.291–292, dated 670–680) has ḻaccina; DHARMA00026 distinguishes this reading from older editorial ḍaccina. ṛ̆assi and ḍappi are displaced, but ḍakkā has a different extension and remains uncertain. Parji/Gadaba killing forms have an explicit alternative d309. Homophonous thirst ḍappi d109 must not be merged solely by spelling.
references: K03 pp.194–195; DEDR 277; Sastri 1969 pp.291–292 inscription16, pp.310–311 inscription38, p.350 index; https://dharmalekha.info/texts/INSTelugu00026
mechanism: Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

boundary_evidence: i-stem and consonantal extensions independently attested; exact historical age of -kar unknown.
input_support: Malayalam aṛ̆ivu and Kannada aṛ̆ipu independently support vowel-first *aẓi; Kannada aṛ̆kaṟ beside akkaṟe directly supplies the relevant medial-cluster comparison.
direction_argument: Kannada preserves both ẓk and kk, favoring assimilation after medial syncope. Telugu akkaṟa remains vowel-initial, so its missing ẓ does not require an earlier initial promotion.
derivation: *aẓi-kar > *aẓkar > akkar gives Telugu akkaṟa and Kannada akkaṟe with regressive assimilation ẓk>kk. *aẓ-ti > arti retains the rhotic-order reflex in another formation; remaining suffix vowels vary independently.
exception_notes: DEDR tentatively relates burn/grieve d276, so root independence needs a sensitivity collapse. Tulu arti has an alternative long-root d381 comparison. Toda arkyn and Kota akm have different final morphology; their exact full derivations are less secure than the initial-order diagnosis.
mechanism: Medial syncope and regressive consonant assimilation, not initial apical displacement

boundary_evidence: u/ay and causative formations independently attested; exact formative vowels for short Pengo and long Kui stems not forced.
input_support: Tamil aṛ̆u/aṛ̆ai, Malayalam aṛ̆uka, Kannada aṛ̆u and Gondi–Konda aṛ- independently establish vowel-first apical and at least u/ay formations. PSS83 pp.14–15 compares *aẓ-u; the database Starostin *jeẓ head is an alternative analysis, not adopted as a given.
direction_argument: Agreement of SD I, Gondi–Konda, Central Dravidian and retained Pengo aṛ- favors earlier V–ẓ. Kui/Kuvi/Manda initial ṛ are innovative under this cognacy, but their ī needs a regional vowel explanation. Pengo causatives supply a within-language original/displaced contrast.
derivation: Retained *aẓ-u > Telugu ēḍu- requires vowel fronting/lengthening before or alongside ẓ>ḍ; ēḍucu has an incorporated past palatal according to K03 p.193. Pengo aṛ-/aṛba versus ṛat/ṛatpa shows apical displacement in causative formations; a possible *aẓ-a-t > ṛat route remains conditional. Kui/Kuvi/Manda *aẓV > ṛī is directionally plausible, but a uniquely supported sequence yielding ī is not yet available.
exception_notes: Telugu long ē does not mean metathesis: the apical is still after the vowel. Pengo ṛatpa is a source correction of earlier aratpa, which would reverse its outcome classification if not followed. Tulu leppuni/leppu/lāvu may involve local aphaeresis/contraction or another root; DEN1 corrects lāvu for earlier levu. Badaga aḷu/avu/au exemplifies lateral lenition/loss. Gondi R Epic aḍusānā could reflect contact and is not needed to establish native retention.
mechanism: Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

boundary_evidence: u plus dental intransitive/transitive extensions independently paired in Tamil/Malayalam.
input_support: Tamil aṛ̆untu/aṛ̆uttu and Malayalam aṛ̆untuka/aṛ̆uttuka independently support high u and transitivity-related dental extensions. Kannada aṛ̆du beside addu preserves an intermediate medial cluster.
direction_argument: Southern high-vowel stems and retained Kannada ẓd provide a direct route to Telugu dd by medial syncope and assimilation. No language in the reviewed set requires initial apical movement.
derivation: *aẓ-unt/utt > *aẓd > addu in Telugu/Kannada; Kannada ajju and Kota aj require an additional local palatal-cluster development. Tulu arduni retains a rhotic-plus-stop cluster. The details of dental voicing/strengthening are conditional, but initial-vowel deletion is unnecessary.
exception_notes: DEDR’s possible link to long-root d396 āẓ could change the remote root quantity; retain that as a sensitivity issue rather than assign long input from an uncertain cross-reference. Gadaba addap blot closely resembles Telugu addu and could be a loan; donor evidence is not explicit, so do not count it as independent phonological confirmation.
mechanism: Medial syncope and cluster assimilation; independent palatal outcomes

boundary_evidence: Low a and labial/dental derivative alternations corroborated independently in SD I.
input_support: Tamil aḷa/aḷavu/aḷappu, Kannada aḷe/aḷavu and Kodagu aḷa independently support low a and postvocalic lateral. Telugu alavi supplies a retained related measure noun.
direction_argument: SD I and retained Telugu alavi support earlier *aḷav rather than initial *lāv with repeated prothesis. Kui/Kuvi/Pengo initial apical forms are therefore innovations under the shared measurement comparison.
derivation: *aḷ-av > *ḷāv > lāvu in Telugu, with separate ḷ>l. Related palatal extensions give Kuvi/Pengo lāc and Kui ḍās/ḍāc, requiring local lateral-to-stop correspondence. Tulu aḷapuni > lappuni is compatible with aphaeresis and strengthening; K03 p.117 explicitly groups its short-vowel counterpart under aphaeresis.
exception_notes: Telugu alavi and lāvu are not independent roots. Tulu short lapp- should not be equated uncritically with Telugu long lāv-. Manda lēc has unexplained e, so quantity/quality tests exclude it pending a supported vowel history. Badaga ādu measured has an explicitly cited archaic aldu precursor, evidence for lateral loss plus contraction/lengthening, not promotion. Toda’s Q in the DEDR digital tense string is a transcription issue; retain raw data and use independent Toda citation for order.
